en: Then, having performed the *śāntika* and *pauṣṭika* fire offerings according to the rules and having personally worshipped the mandala, one should cause the disciples and others to perform worship, saying, "May you all worship the Tathāgatas and the rest according to your ability," and should satisfy those who have entered it with the ritual conduct of the *samaya* according to the rules.
Then,

having performed the peaceful and enriching fire offerings (*śāntika* and *pauṣṭika-homa*) according to the ritual procedure, and having personally made perfect offerings to the mandala, one should cause the disciples and others to perform offerings to the Tathāgatas and so forth in every way as much as they are able. Furthermore,
those who have entered therein should be satisfied with the conduct of the samaya.
In this regard, this is the ritual procedure for the commitment (*samaya*):
First, having prostrated to Vajrasattva and likewise to the Dharma taught by him,
I shall now describe the feast for the Gaṇas, including Vīra and Vīreśvarī.
Having first bowed down to Vajrasattva, the Hero who teaches the Dharma, and the Sovereign Lady of Heroes, I shall explain the communal feast—
the *bhojya*, the *mahābhojya*, the *gaṇacakra*, and the *mahācakra*.
The Niśācakra as proclaimed by Niśi, and likewise the Yakṣālicakraka.
The feast is likewise the great feast; the wheel of the assembly is the great wheel.
The night-wheel is explained as the night; likewise, the garland of directions is the wheel.
The food is common to the Saṅgha; the striking of the gaṇḍī is the great meal.
The gathering of the hosts is the *cakra*; the *mahācakra* is superior to that.
The feast for the Saṅgha is a great feast; the sounding of the gaṇḍī is a great feast. The assembly together is a wheel; that which exceeds it is the Great Wheel.
Thus, [it is held] daily, or monthly, or likewise annually.
On the eighth or the fourteenth day, or on another festival of the Buddha.
Every day, or every month, or likewise every year, or on the eighth, the fourteenth, and other such full lunar days,
one must certainly perform the ritual in Caitra for the sake of guarding the samaya.
One should perform a feast for the Saṅgha and a night-circumambulation for the sake of attaining awakening.
The stūpas are certainly for the purpose of guarding the samaya;
likewise, the nocturnal wheel of the assembly festival should be performed for the sake of accomplishing awakening.

Food is considered to consist of six flavors: that which is chewed (khādya), that which is swallowed (bhojya), that which is bitten (bhakṣya), that which is sipped (prāśya), that which is sucked (coṣya), and that which is licked (lehyaka), along with drinks and the like.
One should prepare food, snacks, as well as items to be chewed, those to be licked, and those to be tasted;
these, along with drinks and so forth, should be presented in autumn, possessing the six flavors and prepared in equal measure.
Having prepared all the necessary ingredients, one should invite [the guests] at the improper time.
Having first prepared the mandala by offering flowers and betel leaves.
Having prepared all the requisites, one should specially invite [the guests] at the appropriate time.
First, having constructed a maṇḍala, one should arrange flowers and tooth-cleansing wood.
Having understood that the Saṅgha is in full assembly, one should present [the offerings] at dawn.
Having honored the Tathāgata with dances, sports, and likewise with musical instruments, they attended upon him.
One should first offer the requisites to the Buddha and the Saṅgha;
likewise, one should honor the Tathāgata with songs and instrumental music.
Then, having made a formal vow, one should begin the communal meal on a patch of ground smeared with cow dung and likewise adorned with flowers and incense.
Furthermore, having made aspirations, one should begin the feast offering for the Saṅgha.
On ground smeared with cow dung, one should prepare seats strewn with flower petals and incense, interspersed with powdered bricks.
And having performed the salutation and other rites for all of them according to their seniority, they sat down.
Having cleared away pebbles and other debris, one should carefully examine the seats.
Having performed prostrations and so forth to all [the Buddhas] in successive order,
those who have restrained body, speech, and mind settle down in their respective places.
Having offered the bali-oblation to Mahākāla, as well as food to Piṇḍola.
Regarding the consumption of alms-food:
sitting properly upon one's seat, with body, speech, and mind perfectly restrained, one should offer the *bali* to Mahākāla; likewise, one should eat the aforementioned food.
To one who desires to eat in his dwelling, one should provide what he requires:
betel, as well as leaves, chalk, and a tooth-stick.
Those who wish to eat in the upper story should likewise be properly seated according to their desire. Having given tooth-cleansers, as well as vessels,
cleansing powder, tooth-sticks, and scented water (*gandhatoya*), one should then give food to the Saṅgha.
Having given the water for sipping and so forth, he should further give a collective fee for the Saṅgha.

Likewise, one should offer the waters of scent; through the accumulation of such giving, there will be wealth. Furthermore, one should offer water for rinsing the mouth and so forth. Having presented offerings to the assembled [deities], the wise and accomplished practitioner should make that merit common to all.
Having paid homage and asked for forgiveness, one should dismiss the meal for the Saṅgha.
The wise and learned should perform all these acts as a common merit;
having prostrated and requested forgiveness, they should request the Saṅgha to depart for their meal.
Thus ends the section on eating.
This refers to the evening meal.
There should be the hearing of the Dharma, as well as the striking of the gong;
there should be an invitation from the elders, and one should invite [the monks] at an improper time.
Likewise, for the Proclaimer of Dharma, as well as for the Elder Upādhyāya and the Invoker of the Special Time,
one should beat the *gaṇḍī* drum.
As before, having propitiated the Sugata and performed unsurpassed worship, [one should proceed].
And one whose mind is fixed on reality should perform the five-fold worship with offerings.
Having invited the Sugatas as before,
one should perform the unsurpassed offerings and the offerings of the five sensory enjoyments, honoring them with that very mind.
Likewise,
there are foods to be chewed, eaten, drunk, licked, and sucked,
as well as seasoned with various flavors, and furthermore, pure rice cooked with fine grains.
Sugar, curd, milk, ghee, jackfruit and other sweet fruits,
flowers, incense, betel leaf, as well as incense smoke and lamps.
Having placed yellow, white, and red cloth, as well as pure robes and so forth,
together with all necessary requisites, within the purified mandala;
For the purpose of reciting the Sūtra of the True Dharma, one should invite the Noble Saṅgha.
Having purified body, speech, and mind, the ritual procedure according to the Vinaya is as follows:
one should perform the offering of water for the feet, the respectful oblation, the water for sipping, and the sprinkling.
The wise elder brother should establish [the lineage] through the various distinctions beginning with the Sthavira.
Furthermore, having placed the sūtra and likewise the articles of worship before him,
the donor, having bowed to that noble Saṅgha of the Indras, should make this request:
The practitioner, holding durvā grass, unhusked rice, parched grain, and flowers in his joined palms,
should repeatedly place his right knee upon the mandala as a support.
Then,
with this verse, [one should honor] the Elder who has attained nirvāṇa through the ordination of a śrāmaṇera,
preceded by the Vajrācārya Guru.
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds;
I rejoice in the merit of the world; I direct my mind toward the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Having recited this noble *Āryasaṃghāṭa-sūtra* and other scriptures,
O Guru, be gracious now for the sake of sentient beings and for my own benefit.

Then the senior lay follower (upāsaka) should present the sūtra to the noble Saṃgha; the members of the Saṃgha should then recite it in order, starting from the elders, out of a desire for excellence.
Once the Sūtra has been recited, one should place it upon the Elder;
having placed the Elder’s seat in front, one should begin that which is appropriate for the Vinaya.
Also according to the sequence of ordination, [the order of seniority] is determined by those such as the newly ordained lay follower (upāsaka).
Having joined his palms in the añjali gesture and placed his knee upon the ground as prescribed.
Having covered [the food] with a fine cloth, one should prostrate with the five limbs;
thereafter, one should begin to eat from such noble assemblies.
Then, even by the laborer-monk who held the same view,
[the food] was offered to the noble Saṃgha according to how the meal had been prepared.
With a handful of flowers, the donor should pray to the Elder and the others:
"O Blessed One! O Noble Saṅgha! Be gracious for my sake!"
Provided with various kinds of food and drink, possessing the most excellent color, fragrance, and flavor—
accept this as it has been obtained and eat it according to your pleasure.
Afterwards, having given water for sipping (ācamana), he should cast the remnants outside;
and for the sake of purification, he should not sweep the area smeared with cow dung and other substances.
One should perform prostration according to the previously mentioned rule;
thereafter, one should worship according to the ritual procedure with the fivefold offerings.
Having given gifts according to one's ability, such as utensils, clothing, and so forth,
one should also cause sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to be bestowed in accordance with the sequence of the recipients.
Preceded by the confession of transgressions, one should likewise perform the rejoicing in merit and the generation of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) preceded by the maṇḍala.
May the Perfectly Awakened Ones, the Saṅgha, and the other supreme assemblies of noble ones deign to forgive [me].
Grant me the fruit as desired, and perfect Buddhahood.
The welfare of all sentient beings has been accomplished for you; having granted you success according to your aspirations, go now to the realm of the Buddhas, and return once more.
One should cause the assembly of noble elders and others to bestow blessings;
and with verses on generosity, one should inspire the donor toward the exaltation of the Buddha.
One should constantly recite the Three Refuges and offer flowers and water.
By this ritual procedure, the donor should dismiss the entire Saṅgha. Thus ends the ritual for the feast of the True Dharma.
In accordance with the previously mentioned procedure, a communal meal is properly prepared;
meanwhile, there is the sounding of musical instruments such as the mṛdaṅga, dundubhi, bherī, and ghaṇṭā.
One should offer a counter-meal in palaces, mango groves, and pleasure gardens;
in royal palaces and mansions, one should employ speech characterized by humility. Thus ends the rule for the counter-meal.
By striking the Dharma-gong and likewise by blowing the conch shell,
it is proclaimed that the entire Saṅgha of the Cailakas shall partake of the communal meal.
On days, in fortnights, in months, in seasons,
and in years, those endowed with faith give to the Saṅghas.
One should offer food during an eclipse of Rāhu, at the transition of the sun into a new sign, and at the end of a day;
those who give food to the noble assembly shall obtain inexhaustible fruit.

One should always worship Padmottara and the other ten Buddhas, as well as those Buddhas whose sphere of activity is the beginning and the end, and all others such as the five Buddhas, placing them at the forefront.
One should carry out the ritual according to the previously stated procedure by means of the officiant;
at the beginning, middle, and end, one should strike the Dharma-gong.
One should move around the food mandala in the sequence of beginning, middle, and end;
at the conclusion, after the dismissal of those who have eaten, [the leftovers] are offered according to the ten assemblies in their natural order.

At the commencement of the meal, one should dismiss the ten members of the Saṅgha and cause them to enter again. At the conclusion of the Buddhasvarūpa [mantra], it should be known that the donor and the supplicants are [one]. Thus ends the ritual for the communal meal of the Saṅgha.
In a well-concealed, solitary, and delightful place, free from all wicked beings;
within the pure interior of a monastery or palace, one should perform the *gaṇacakra*.
Always by a riverbank, in a forest, in a bower, at a sacred seat (*pīṭha*), in a grove, or on a mountain.
One should arrange the gaṇacakra when one is completely free from all defects.
On a pure ground smeared with cow dung, covered by an excellent canopy,
where a lotus of the world has been placed upon a beautiful universal vajra;
A beautiful woman, consecrated by wisdom, born of the five families,
auspicious and endowed with artistic qualities— one should invite her with an offering of flowers.
Accompanied by auspicious sounds and with water mixed with fragrance,
the donor should wash the feet and enter according to the order of seniority.

Having mastered the teachings through the *saṃvidyā* [of the goddesses], the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśvara), having fully discerned the merits and defects of all the heroes beginning with Niśā, should bring them under his control.
One who is wrathful, unrestrained, greedy, evil-minded, a deceiver of sentient beings,
hostile toward the guru, and envious of superior qualities should not act as a leader of the maṇḍala.
One who is difficult to subdue, stubborn, deluded, established in asceticism, a heretic, or dull-witted—
even if he be one's own son— should not be consecrated nor allowed to enter the Gaṇacakra.
Mastering the arts of wisdom and skillful means, awakening to all phenomena,
and possessing the excellence of peaceful form and qualities— may he act as the leader of the assembly.
The steadfast one who holds the vajra and bell, the foremost among those possessing the qualities of a mendicant teacher,
pervading the minds of all sentient beings and knowing reality, should engage [the disciple] in service.

Having been authorized through the secret signs (cchomā) and other rites, one who is proficient in the ten principles and a knower of all ritual arts shall become the leader of the mandala (cakranāyaka).
By means of the yoga of instantaneous visualization, the wise Vajrācārya should perform the binding of the directions for the purpose of destroying all malevolent beings.
The mantra: Oṃ, to Niśābhairava! Ciri 2, siri 2, khiri 2! By means of the form of Kirāta, bind the mouths of snakes and the like! Hūṃ svāhā!
For the purpose of binding the mouths of the wicked, one should recite [the mantra] twenty-one times over four pieces of clod of earth and cast them into the corners.
Then, with a joyful heart, one should perform the complete worship of the heroic Vīreśvarīs who have taken refuge at the feet of the Guru,
[offering them] golden garments, flowers, garlands, crowns, and ornaments for the limbs.
The intoxicating [drink], fragrant with the scent of lotuses, was enchanted and variegated with gold.
Smeared with the five fragrances— sandalwood produced in Malaya, the pollen of saffron and *sihlaka*, and blended with musk.
Abundant varieties of flowers, powdered incense, various fruits as offerings, and diverse kinds of lamps and incense.
The vessel is white, born of the letter Ā, filled with water, lotuses, and the contents of Mount Meru and Yama;
its temple is marked by the eight signs of the sacred fields.
Hūṃ! [The chariot] with five banners of the wind of birth.
[He who possesses] the *Svākārajātoragarājasūtra*, [who has] rice born from the seed-syllable *hāḥ*, a variegated garland, [and] whose mind is free from marks (*alakṣaka*), who has three eyes,
[and who is the master] of the red-marked *Prayāga* and of *Varuṇa* marked with a fish.
At Kolāgira, the mark is human flesh; at Aṭṭahāsa, it is lac-dye.
At Upavīta and Jayantī, it is the *caritra* (footprint) for all castes.
At Koṭivarṣa, it is a flour-mark, possessing a banner of ten million deities.
The seed-syllables: Svāhā, Raṃ, Uṃ, Oṃ, Hrīṃ, Khaṃ, Hūṃ. Om.
Empowered by the eight signs. || O || The installation of the offering. || O ||
[An arrow] may be made of ruby, gold, silver, iron, bamboo,
reed, stone, metal, wood, fruit, or bone; or it may be made of horn, glass, tortoise-shell, horn, mother-of-pearl, or conch-shell.
A leaf-cup made from the skin of a *kaṃsa* snake, and a skull-bowl made from human skin.
One should take up the supreme vessel, which is free from all defects, endowed with all the auspicious marks, and as described at the beginning of the tantric texts.
The Instruction on the Alms Bowl. || O ||
One should visualize the offering substances as mixed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
or as unguents for the limbs and so forth, or as wine mixed with the nectar of lamps.

Sandalwood, musk, camphor, and saffron are the medicinal ingredients; yellow sandalwood is the collection of requisites for accomplishing spiritual success, characterized as the means for attaining the essence.
One should properly collect the ten substances according to the prescribed rule:
[the substance] born from a hero’s corpse, and furthermore, cow-dung ash.
The five nectars (pañcāmṛta), cow products such as milk and so forth, and the hero-substances (vīra) and so forth serve as the illuminating lamp;
one should likewise blend these together with perfume and the powdered ingredients.
Having purified each [substance] individually with its respective seed-syllable, one should mix them together;
or else, one should fashion pills the size of a chickpea seed.
VUṂ ĀṂḤ HRĪṂ KHAṂ HUṂ || The consecration of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Oṃ trāṃ jrīṃ khaṃ huṃ. This is the purification of the five lamps. Oṃ.
The exposition of the ten substances. || 0 ||
Medicines derived from bipeds, quadrupeds, birds, and those born from eggs; as well as fat, flesh, meat, and the savory meat of wild game.
The *baladharitrī* and *tariṣa* should be known as those fashioned for expulsion;
one should cause them to circulate in this very manner within the wheel of the Hero and the Mistress of Heroes. ||o||
Flesh.
Aliprasannā, Madirāmṛta, Sudhā, Pīyūṣa, Gadāṅkā, Māmakī,
Balapradā, Sarmada, Somavāruṇī.
Rasāsavābjā and Madhucāriṇī. ||o||
The perception of intoxicants. || O ||

The Victors have declared that there are three primary types of what is called "intoxicant": that made from flour, that made from molasses, and that made from honey; these are distinguished by their source, their place of attainment, and their specific characteristics.
Seated upon a lordly serpent born from the syllable *naṃ*,
within a vessel containing the mandala of Varuṇa born from the syllable *vaṃ*,
[it is] with pieces of priyaṅgu, black pepper, aguru, and kuṣṭha— dear to the young.
Having thoroughly perfumed it, [he beholds] the ocean of nectar filled with wine.
One should place the vessel for the bees, adorned with flower-garlands, sacred threads, vermilion, and red lac,
as well as with externally applied fragrant unguents.
The instruction for the placement of the honey-pitcher. || o ||
° Sthāpana: Oṃ āḥ hūṃ || Oṃ ha hoḥ hrīṃ aḥ svāhā ||
The syllable *ha* removes color; the syllable *ho* destroys fragrance;
the syllable *hrīṃ* is the destroyer of virility; and *aḥ* is filled with nectar.
With the mantra for the extraction of nectar, having covered [the area] twenty-one times— thrice seven—
one should recite this mantra while pressing with two saws.
Oṃ amṛte amṛtasambhave ehy ehi amṛtaṃ praveśaya hrīḥ hūṃ || o ||
The mantra for the presiding deity of taste. || O ||
Oṃ hūṃ juṃ ghruṃ śruṃ hruṃ svāhā.
The mantra for consecrating vessels for liquor. || O ||
The liquor empowered by this [mantra], filled with the extracted soma and bubbling within the belly of the jar, should be distributed among all the heroes.
With beautiful women whose hearts were filled with joy at the sight of Kāliñjara bowing down, who smiled with playful grace,
and whose hands were like tender sprouts from which the nectar of the Siddhas flowed;
One should cause the nectar to circulate, joined with the hook and the five [factors].
Behold! Abandoning the pride of caste, one should practice the Dharma;
for the Brahmin, the dog, and the outcaste are all equal in their essential nature. ||o||
The grasping of the five hooks. || 0 ||
Obeisance to that one who has gone beyond the conduct of worldly dharma and is free from the cycle of rebirth; he is devoid of both the literal and the figurative meaning of the Gāthās.
Oṃ! Svāgata! Dharma! Anaghu! Cāpaṣalāpagateṇa!
Paṇamaha tattie! Oṃ!
The mention of "intoxicants" (madya). || 0 ||
% Catuṣpīṭha Apabhraṃśa verse:
oṃ āḥ hrīṃ khaṃ hūṃ ||
One should bathe [the deity] with the five-fold vessel.
Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature.
Oṃ, all phenomena are vajra-pure; I am vajra-pure.
Oṃ, all phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga.
Having thus recited the three purities and drunk three mouthfuls of *ghuḍhuka*, [one should proceed].
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra that tastes the nectar of all Tathāgatas. Oṃ.
The Instruction on the Taste of Immortality. || O ||

Then, having sat down and performed the threefold meditative absorption (samādhi) upon one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), and having worshipped thoroughly with various flower garlands, collyrium, vermilion, ornaments, and so forth, one should set in motion the *gaṇacakra* accompanied by the heroes (vīra) and heroines (vīreśvarī).
According to the procedure prescribed for the *gaṇacakra*, one should present various kinds of food and drink,
including curd, milk, ghee, sugar-candy, and cooked dishes.
And there was rice with all its condiments, each portion topped with a supreme morsel;
from the novices to the elders, it was served along with small cups of *vāruṇī* wine.
Taking the offering, one should worship at the side of Bali;
with the mantra for all spirits, one should satisfy those outside.
In the place of the Vīra, Vīrā, and Vīreśvarī, outside the maṇḍala in the courtyard,
the wise one should cause [the offering] to be given facing the threshold at the location of its door.
I bow with devotion to all the Vīras and Vīreśvarīs who dwell in the seats (pīṭhas), secondary seats (upapīṭhas), fields (kṣetras), assemblies (melās), and cremation grounds (śmaśānas). ||o||
Then the patron, having prepared a mandala with fragrant water, should pray in this manner with his hands joined in a gesture of reverence (*añjali*) holding flowers,
using the verse beginning with "yo 'mṛta-gāmī" and so forth.
One should conceive of the fivefold conduct as being of a single color;
with a mind and self free from conceptual construction, one should enjoy it according to one's pleasure. ||o||

At that time, the yogi who has spoken thus succeeds regarding caste and non-caste, pure and impure, edible and inedible, drinkable and undrinkable, afflicted and unafflicted, sweet and bitter, existence and non-existence, and the distinct and the non-distinct; he succeeds through the net of conceptualization, and not otherwise.
Thus, one should abandon all doubts regarding the maṇḍala-circles (*cchandoha-cakras*).
With various dances and songs, the playing of lutes and flutes,
and the distribution of offerings to the *ali* spirits, one should set in motion the circle of heroes (*vīra-cakra*).
Having drawn a mandala before it, the donor, who is devoted to those who possess faith,
should seek out the wheel-mandala for the sake of accomplishing all aims and desires;
this is extracted from the assembly of heroes beginning with the illustrious *Samāja*, *Carasaṃvara*, *Heruka*, and *Śrīyogāmbara*.

The Yoga is that which is peaceful, nourished by the consumption of the fangs of the net of conceptual constructions, and is the foremost wheel of the innate assembly of Buddhas of the Universal Self.
Having placed the moon and sun within [the maṇḍala] and purified it in all its colors,
one should meditate upon that which is composed of the seed-syllables beginning with Oṃ, Śrīṃ, Jriṃ, Ghriṃ, and Hūṃ;
though distinguished by five colors, one should contemplate it as being of a single color.
Having recited [the mantra] seven times with the three syllables, one should cause it to circulate by means of nectar.
For the sake of protecting the accomplishment of all aims, one should distribute the offering (*bali*).
One should distribute it according to one's pleasure for the gratification of the external and internal deities.
One should meditate on a lotus, above which is a wide vessel produced from the seed-syllable Ā,
its interior filled with the nectar of the five gnoses;
and upon that vessel, a *ḍhakka* drum produced from the moon of the syllable OṂ, topped by a vajra.
Hūṃ jaṃ: from the fluid of the white khaṭvāṅga comes the elixir of accomplishment.
Impelled by the wind of the syllable *yaṃ* and cooked by the fire of existence (*bhavāgni*),
one should contemplate the ten substances there— food and so forth— as the five products of the cow (*gokudahanavīra*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and the lamp.
[The practitioner] should emanate [the deities] arising from the seed-syllables VAṂ ĀḤ JIṂ KHAṂ HŪṂ LĀṂ MĀṂ PĀṂ TĀṂ,
produced from the seed-syllable HŪṂ, by means of the vajra-tongue.
One should then invoke the gnosis-beings (jñānasattva), the external and internal deities.

One should please [the deities] with the five types of ritual offerings (*pañcopacārapūjā*) and with the *lāsya* dance and so forth. The Buddha [is pleased] by the offering (*bali*) within the lotus-heart of the mouths of the gods and asuras. The gift of the remains (*utsiṣṭadāna*), however, is the wheel of offering (*balipradānacakra*), at the time when the propitiation is complete.
With his mouth filled by the delusion of internal accomplishment, from the cavities of his mouth which have internalized the flames,
he should perform the rite with the sound of the vajra-bell mingled with the resonance of the mantra, accompanied by fragrant lamps and blazing fire-offerings,
using either the verses beginning with the *Subāhu-tantra* or the mantras arranged according to the sequence of one's own maṇḍala.

Oṃ! Having touched and purified the full vessel of the great bali offering with three peaks blossomed by the rays of infinite moons, one should again swiftly employ the upward-rising crest-flames, sun-rays, and side-glances for the purpose of devouring.
One should offer water for rinsing the mouth, betel, a lamp, and an incense stick before the principal deity using the root mantra; the remainder should be removed elsewhere.

Piercing through all forms and so forth, the single consciousness within the three realms—the uninterrupted bliss of the true yogins—is also exceedingly powerful. [This is] the offering of the *bali*.
Having approached and performed a dance with folded hands to please the Heroines beginning with Cakreśvarī,
Karmavajrā— without joining her palms individually before each of them— should request that they perform the rite of dismissal (*visarjana*).
When the command "Let it be done" has been given, starting from the youngest and ending with the eldest, [the rite is performed].
Having taken the remnant-ball (ucchiṣṭapiṇḍa), one should place it before the leader of the assembly (gaṇādhyakṣa).
Furthermore, one should place there the remains of food, as well as the powder from the vessel and flowers from all around;
and upon that, one should again add a small amount of cooked rice or condiments. ||o||
... thus it was instructed in the upper margin by a second hand: "... thereupon, [he], being composed...
Henceforth, the text is restored in parallel with the Tibetan;
this makes it very clear that the Tibetan translator either saw this manuscript or one closely related to it!

Thereafter, being composed in meditative absorption, he sees Ucchiṣṭavajra with his retinue, appearing in forms such as those for pacification and so forth, having been summoned and extending both hands for the purpose of drinking. Having gathered excellent food from before the universal monarchs and brought it therein, and having offered the samaya-incense and other offerings, he then recites the mantra while extending both hands toward his mouth; by filling the mouth with nectar, he satiates Ucchiṣṭavajra and his retinue, whereupon they become pleased.
It manifests a dream in which it is being honored along with its retinue, and it accomplishes the task.

Having invited the remaining Vajra together with the wheel, and visualizing the two hands fully extended for the purpose of drinking in peaceful and other forms, one should take up the specific recitations in front of the revolving wheel, cause [the deity] to enter therein, and offer the samaya perfumes and so forth.

Then, while reciting the mantra, one should extend both hands close to the mouth and sprinkle it with the mouth full of nectar; by this, the remaining vajra together with his retinue will be pleased. One will see him and his retinue in dreams, and they will also carry out their activities.

In this regard, the mantra is as follows: *oṃ kuru 2 vattali 2 mahāvattali siddhamukhi śmaśānavāsini pretamukhi caṇḍakarāli rudhirapriye samayārakṣi yogeśvari kili 2 rāve pitṛvanamadhye bhuñjaha bhakkhaha saha gaṇadūte dhūmāṅgāri caṇḍakarāli tiṣṭha svīkuru 2 hūṃ gṛhṇa 2 sarvaduṣṭān bhakṣa 2 hoḥ phreṃ hreṃ amukasya sarvavighnaśāntiṃ kuru phaṭ svāhā*.
Thus ends the mantra for the offering of all leftover food.

In that regard, the mantra is as follows: Oṃ kuru kuru vattali vattali mahā-vattali siddhimukhe | smaśāna-vāsini pretamukhe | smaśāna-vāsini pretamukhe | caṇḍakāri rudhiraprīye | samayarakṣi yogambari | kilakila | rāve pitṛvanamadhye | bhujahabhakha ha | sahagana rudhe |

DHŪMĀṂGARI CAṆḌAKHĀRI TIṢṬHA SVIKURU KURU HŪṂ | GṚHṆA GṚHṆA SARVA DUṢṬĀN BHAKṢA BHAKṢA HOḤ PHEṂ PHEṂ CHE GE MO’I SARVA VIGHNĀN ŚĀNTAṂ KURU KURU PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. This is the mantra for the remaining *bali* offering in all cases.
Then, having offered water for sipping (ācamana) there with fragrant water,
one should offer perfume, flowers, and betel-leaves, beginning with the preceptor (ācārya).
Then,
fragrant water for rinsing the mouth should be offered there;
having presented perfumes, flowers, and tooth-wood, the preceptor should go first.
Having recited the verse on generosity and dedicated its fruit,
one should give a fee according to one's ability and dismiss the circle of the assembly (gaṇacakra).
Recite the verses on generosity; fully dedicate its fruit.
Having offered the gift according to one's ability, request the assembly to depart from the maṇḍala.
Regarding that, the verses on generosity are as follows:

Regarding that, the verse on generosity is as follows: "The Lord of Speech has declared that an offering made to those in the animal realm yields a hundredfold merit; to one who is sinful, a thousandfold; to a human being, a hundredfold; and to those rich in ethical discipline, a hundred-thousandfold."
When one has attained detachment from external desires, a gift given to those standing on the path yields a hundred times ten million; furthermore, it becomes a source of immeasurable fruit.
The Lord of Speech has declared that for those in the animal realms, the merit is a hundredfold; for sinful humans, it is ten thousandfold;
for those endowed with ethical discipline, it is a hundred-thousandfold;
and for those who abide in detachment from external desires, it is ten billionfold.
For those established on the path, it further bestows the fruit of the immeasurables;
through this merit, having attained all-seeing vision and having conquered the enemies that are the afflictions—
May I deliver the world from the ocean of existence, which is agitated by the great waves of old age, disease, and death.
Thus ends the dedication of merit in the *Jātakamālā*, chapter 8.55.
By this merit, may I attain the state of the All-Seeing One and, having conquered the enemy of defects,
may I deliver all beings from the ocean of existence, which is turbulent with the great waves of old age,
sickness, and death. Thus ends the *Gaṇacakra*.
"By these [verses], one should fully dedicate the merit"—this refers to the gaṇacakra.
If this very same [rite] is performed outside in a cremation ground by Kāliñjala masters, it is called the Mahācakra.
Having gone outside from this very place, while performing [the rites] in the charnel ground,
the qualified master should recite the *Mahācakra*:
"Flower, incense, likewise lamp, perfume, garland, and clothing."
But one should offer whatever food and drink are available.
Flowers, incense, lamps, and likewise perfumes, garlands, and scents;
one should also properly arrange whatever drinks and foods are available.
Then, one should place the vessel of intoxicants in the center, keeping it steady.
Having invoked the wheel of Māmakī and honored it, one should cause it to enter.
In the center, place a vessel for drinking; therein, it should be set without moving.
Having invited the remaining wheel and paid homage to it, one should install it;
above that, a skull-cup endowed with the [proper] characteristics should be placed.
One should cause [the disciple] to worship and offer flowers, incense, and so forth to the Karmavajrī.
Upon that, one should place a skull-cup possessing the required characteristics;
the practitioner of the Karma-vajra should offer flowers, incense, and other such offerings.
Furthermore, the five nectars and the five grains should be consecrated again with the mantra.
One should cast it into the entire collection [of ritual materials] through the yoga of the deity's form.
Having consecrated the five nectars and the five meats with mantra,
one should again arrange all the ritual requisites. Through the yoga of the deity’s form,
one should prepare the drinking vessel, such as the skull-cup of Viśvāmitra and others.
All food, drink, and so forth, here as well, are exactly as they were before.
One should thoroughly examine skull-cups and other vessels for drinking, such as those belonging to various spiritual friends.
All food, drink, and so forth, here are just as they were before.
Because the mantra exists in a liquid form, it is known as "mantra-drink."
One whose self is united with the deity of the mantra should perform the drinking of the mantra.
Because it is of the nature of the essence of mantra, it is remembered as the "mantra-drink.
I, the practitioner of the yoga of the mantra deity, truly partake of the mantra-drink.
One should dismiss the *gaṇacakra* after having offered betel nuts and other such items.
Having prostrated before the Guru with devotion, they depart to their respective places.
One should perform the request for departure of the gaṇacakra and offer the fruits, such as *go-yu* and so forth.
Having prostrated with devotion to the Guru, one requests them to depart to their respective abodes.
Thus ends the Mahācakra.
Thus it is called the Great Wheel.
One should perform the nocturnal rite in mountain caves and thickets, on the shores of the great ocean, or in gardens, forests, and ponds.
In mountain caves, medicinal valleys, on seashores, in pleasure groves, in forests,
or even in courtyards, one should properly undertake the cycle of night practices.
[One should consume] the five nectars and the five grains, which are auspicious and consist of the five Buddhas.
Seated upon the five seats, he is established in the five families.
The five nectars and the five meats are virtuous, being the very nature of the five Buddhas.
Seated in equipoise upon the five seats, one abides within the purity of the five families.
A yogin who has practiced the secret signs (*cchomma*) and the intentional language (*saṃdhyā*) should arrive [at the feast].
Having offered a seat for him in front, one should commence the circle of the night.
One should apply oneself to the signs and the intentional meaning. When the yogi himself has arrived, first provide him with a seat and begin the entire wheel of the night.
For the ritual action, there are the four wrathful deities at the four gates, along with Sumbha and Uṣṇīṣa.
The yoginīs, such as Rūpavajrā and the others, should be established in their respective locations.

At the four gates are the four wrathful deities; Ghaṇṭāpāla and Uṣṇīṣa perform their functions. Rūpavajrā and the other yoginīs are to be placed in their respective positions. The Ācārya [should sit] upon a human skin, and the others likewise upon cowhide and so forth.
But one who is free from doubt and possesses pure intellect should worship the pentad of Buddhas.
Regarding the ritual union (*candhi*):
the master [should worship] with human skin, and others [should worship] with cowhide and so forth;
with a mind of purity during the night, they should make offerings to the five Buddhas.
Seated upon the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and other locations, equal to the heroes and the mistresses of heroes,
may you now certainly preside over this circle out of compassion for me.
The heroes and heroines who abide in equipoise upon thrones and the like are equal;
then, one should consecrate the wheel with stable compassion in equipoise.
Having recited the verse three times, one should scatter flowers and other offerings upward.
Then, having prostrated to them again and again, he should invite them.
By reciting the verses three times and scattering flowers and other offerings above, one should then invite the deities; repeatedly [employing] the mudrās,
having made the night-circle (niśācakra) manifest, one should cause the wisdom-circle (jñānacakra) to enter.
The yogi, whose nature is Mañjuvajra, should worship the maṇḍala of the Victors.
Having clarified the wheel of night, one should thoroughly enter the wheel of gnosis;
the yogin should worship the maṇḍala of the nature of Mañjuvajra.
Having worshipped the circle of yoginīs, bliss shall not perish.
One should arrange the movement there by means of the application of left and right.
Having made offerings, one should not abandon the joy of the Yoginīcakra;
through the union of the right and the non-right, all conduct therein should be examined.
That which is taught in the Yoginī and Yoga Tantras regarding the gathering of the assembly (gaṇamelaka), [should be practiced].
The Guru, who is conversant with the rules of the samaya conduct, should perform the worship according to that ritual procedure.
In the Yoga and Yoginī Tantras, whatever assemblies of the *gaṇacakra* have been taught— those assemblies are to be honored by the Guru who is learned in the conduct of the commitments (*samaya*).
The Tathāgatas are to be worshipped through the purification of the five aspects;
thus the yogi, filled with compassion, certainly acts for the benefit of sentient beings.

One should worship the Tathāgatas with the fivefold purity; the yogi who has entered into compassion must certainly act for the benefit of sentient beings. Having established the vajra in the lotus, one should not emit the bodhicitta.
In that regard, the reality to be realized is, in truth, distinguished by bliss and so forth.
By remaining in the state of the vajra-lotus, one should not emit the bodhicitta;
there, through the suchness of the distinctions of joy and so forth, one realizes it as suchness.
Having abandoned all conceptual thought, with a mind focused on the form of the deity—
Yogis should abide therein by means of a non-conceptual nature.
Having completely abandoned all conceptual intentions, the yogi should abide there within the nature of non-conceptuality, contemplating the form of the deity.
In such a nocturnal wheel (*niśācakra*), there is nothing whatsoever to be avoided.
A mother, a sister, a daughter, and a sister’s daughter.
From the ritual of the Night Wheel, there is no exclusion whatsoever:
the wet-nurse, the sister, the daughter, the granddaughter, and likewise the wife of Māmaka, as well as one's own sister.
The sister of one's father and the sister of one's mother, as well as the eight Prajñās, bestow excellent accomplishment.
Prajñā,
Ātmikā, likewise Kanyā, Mātṛkā, and similarly Pitṛsvasṛ—
these eight Prajñās bestow the supreme accomplishment.
The worship of these [deities] should be performed through the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*;
thus, O Buddha, the entire essence of the Buddhas must be realized again and again.
As for the ritual of making offerings to them, having applied [the mantra] to the bola and kakka,
one should personally and repeatedly realize Buddhahood itself as all Buddhas;
there is no recitation of mantras, no asceticism, and no fire-offerings.
Neither the mandala-dweller nor the mandala itself;
that alone is the recitation of mantra, that is austerity, that is the fire-oblation,
and that is both the mandala-dweller and the mandala.
In brief, he is one whose form is the assembly of mind.
There is no mantra recitation, no asceticism, and no fire offering;
there is neither the possessor of the maṇḍala nor the maṇḍala itself.
That is mantra recitation, that is austerity, and that is fire offering;
that is the possessor of the maṇḍala and the maṇḍala itself—
in brief, the mind is the very embodiment of the assembly.
The conduct described as being of terrifying form is not taught for the sake of enjoyment;
rather, it is for the purpose of examining one's own mind: is the mind stable or is it wavering?
Is the mind stable or wavering? Examine your own mind individually.

Regarding what was taught as the conduct of one possessing a terrifying form for the sake of enjoyments—whether external or internal—in such a nocturnal wheel (*niśācakra*), the excellent disciple is consecrated once again.
Through the power of cultivation, accomplishment shall be attained in this very life.
By such a ritual, during the cycle of the night, he is consecrated once more by the Wise One (Buddha).
Through the power of meditation, the siddhi arises within this very existence.
Even if one should not perform the meditation and so forth for even a moment, nevertheless, that [siddhi] occurs.
There would be no offense if that accomplishment were achieved within seven lifetimes.

Likewise, here in this practice of meditation and so forth, even if one performs little or nothing at all, if there is no downfall, one will attain accomplishment in the seventh [life]. Aho! The power of the skillful means of those who well follow the Mahāyāna!
Having embraced their beloveds tightly, they enjoy the god whose banner is a sea-monster.
"O, having well arrived at the Mahāyāna through skillful means and power,
one should embrace the passionate woman firmly and serve the deity of desire.
Having offered the *bali*, worship, and so forth as before, one should dismiss the wheel (*cakra*).
Having paid homage to the Lord of the Mandala, they dwell in happiness as they please.
Having performed the torma offerings and other rites as before, one requests the wheel to depart.
After prostrating to the Lord of the Wheel, one should remain in whatever way is comfortable.
Thus concludes the Night Wheel.
Thus is the night wheel.
The skillful one should make an appointment at a watering place, or in the middle of a village, or outside a mandala hall; there the adept should give the yakṣālika offering.
One should observe the commitments of the *thung-gcod*; furthermore, [this should be done] either in the center of a village, or...
Furthermore, outside the mandala house, the wise one should provide a row of ground plots.
One should not look at anyone's face, nor should one ask any questions of anyone;
for beings of various forms indeed gather there.
One should not look at the face at all, nor should one regard it as being anything else whatsoever.
When sentient beings have certainly come there in various forms,
Having offered a welcome to those who have arrived, one should prepare the vessel for the yantra.
What is the leaf for food? One should give them all food, drink, and so forth, according to their desire.
Having arrived, one should say "Welcome"; one should carefully examine the leaves or vessels;
one should provide them with food, drink, and so forth; and one should do everything according to their wishes.
The adept should offer three oblations at the beginning, middle, and end;
having offered betel, incense, flowers, and so forth, he should dismiss the maṇḍala.
At the beginning, middle, and end, the wise should offer three bali offerings.
Having offered medicinal substances, perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one requests the Wheel [of Dharma] to depart.
Thus ends the cycle of the Yakṣa-ali.
This refers to the wheel of the cycle of arguments (*digvarga-cakra*).
At whatever time all the yoginīs are on the left side of the Mistress of the Wheel (cakreśvarī), there is a single means for the sake of bliss; that is the wheel of the Vīreśvarīs.

If all the *samayas* have become yoginīs and there is a single means on the left side of the *cakreśvarī* for the sake of bliss, then it is the wheel of the *vīreśvarī*.
But where all the heroes are on the left of the Lord of the Circle (cakreśvara) and there is only one yoginī for the sake of bliss, that is the Hero’s Circle (vīracakra).
Where all have become heroes and, for the sake of bliss, there is a single yoginī to the left of the Lord of the Wheel, that is the Wheel of Heroes (*vīracakra*).
These two wheels may be used even during the day in a pleasant, windowless room, provided it is after two watches have passed.
One should understand that these two wheels should be practiced for at least two sessions daily in a house free from cracks, even during the spring season.
Therefore,
if there were not a single wisdom and a single means for the two wheels of the Hero and the Mistress of Heroes, then there would be a reversal of the merit of the lord of the gift.
Without the bliss of wisdom and means, one does not attain the state of being a *cakra* at all;
for it is the word of the Blessed One that "a *cakra* devoid of wisdom is merely a gathering of commoners (*bhaṇḍamelaka*)."

“Without the bliss of wisdom and method, the wheel does not become the means. That wheel which is deficient in wisdom is without conflict; it is the wheel of union. This is the word of the Blessed One.
Thus concludes the procedure for the *gaṇacakra*.
This is the ritual for the gaṇacakra.
